Main.sentence: Much ___E:Buddhist art U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist_art)___ uses depictions of the historical Buddha, ___E:Gautama Buddha U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gautama_Buddha)___ , which are known as Buddharūpa ( lit. ' Form of the Awakened One ' ) in ___E:Sanskrit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit)___ and ___E:Pali U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pali)___ .
These may be statues or other images such as paintings.

The main figure in an image may be someone else who has obtained ___E:Buddhahood U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhahood)___ , or a ___E:boddhisattva U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boddhisattva)___ , especially in the various traditions of ___E:Mahayana Buddhism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahayana_Buddhism)___ .

Other ___E:Buddhas and bodhisattvas in art U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhas_and_bodhisattvas_in_art)___ have become increasingly common over the centuries, perhaps now outnumbering images of the historical Buddha.

In its first centuries ___E:Buddhism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism)___ was ___E:largely or entirely aniconic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aniconism_in_Buddhism)___ , not showing the person of Buddha except by symbols and relics.

This changed, and figures of the Buddha became very common in the ___E:art of Gandhara U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_of_Gandhara)___ and ___E:Gupta art U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_art)___ .
As forms of ___E:esoteric Buddhism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esoteric_Buddhism)___ developed, other figures from the expanding array of Buddhist sacred persons became more prominent.

In ___E:Theravada Buddhism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theravada_Buddhism)___ this was much less the case, and figures of the historical Buddha remain the most common main images in temples and shrines to the present.

Early images were most often of Buddha standing, but seated meditating postures, essentially the ___E:lotus position U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lotus_position)___ of ___E:yoga U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoga)___ , came to predominate.
Often these represent a specific moment in the Buddha's life, which is identified by the Buddha's hand gesture ( mudra ), or attributes shown.
There are also statues of the ___E:Reclining Buddha U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reclining_Buddha)___ , lying down, usually showing the moment of his death.

Sets of ___E:narrative scenes from the life of the Buddha U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_of_Buddha_in_art)___ tend to concentrate on standard groupings such as the ___E:Eight Great Events U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Eight_Great_Events_in_the_Life_of_Buddha)___ or other sets, but may be much larger.

Originally common in ___E:reliefs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relief)___ , and probably paintings of which few have survived, they have more recently mostly been in painted form. Narrative scenes may show the Buddha in various poses, though they tend to show the Buddha in the same standing, seated or lying positions, with other figures or a mudra indicating what moment is being depicted.
Despite cultural and regional differences in the interpretations of texts about the life of Gautama Buddha, there are some general guidelines to the attributes of a Buddharupa:
The elongated earlobes are vestiges of his life as a prince, when he wore extravagant jewelry.
The bump at the top of the head is the ___E:ushnisha U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ushnisha)___ and represents spirituality, wisdom, and awakening.
Depictions of the Buddha vary widely across cultures.

The image of Buddhas started to emerge from the first century CE in ___E:North India U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_India)___ , developed in ___E:Gandhara U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gandhara)___ and ___E:Mathura U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathura)___ .

The art of Gandhara was influenced by ___E:Ancient Greek art U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_art)___ , leading to the development of ___E:Greco-Buddhist art U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Buddhist_art)___ with anatomically well-proportioned and realistic figure of the Buddha.

One of the most influential Buddhist art was ___E:Gupta U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_Empire)___ art and the later ___E:Amaravati U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amaravati_mandal,_Andhra_Pradesh)___ style.

From India the depiction of Buddha spread to the rest of Asia. The Buddharupas of India, Sri Lanka, Javanese ___E:Sailendra U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borobudur)___ and ___E:Cambodian art U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambodian_art)___ usually depict a well-proportioned figure, but sometimes he is shown emaciated, in recollection of the Buddha's years of ascetic practices.

Many people may be familiar with the "Happy" or "Laughing" Buddha, a different historical figure, who should not be confused with the images of Gautama Buddha. ___E:Budai U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budai)___ , a Chinese Buddhist monk also known as Hotei , is depicted as fat and happy, almost always shown smiling or laughing, and is associated with ___E:Maitreya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maitreya)___ , the future Buddha.
A statue or a painting of Buddha always illustrates a mudra or gesture.
There are large numbers of these, but a few are the oldest and most common.

In ___E:Mahayana Buddhism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahayana_Buddhism)___ , some of the most common have also become identified with the five transcendental Buddhas, also called " ___E:Dhyani Buddhas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhyani_Buddha)___ " or "Pancha Buddhas", further complicating identification of the figure shown.
These mudras are as follows:

Images of ___E:Buddha U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gautama_Buddha)___ showing him reclining, represent his Parinirvana or departure into final ___E:nirvana U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nirvana)___ at death.
Other times he is holding various symbolic objects, or making symbolic ___E:mudras U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mudra)___ (gestures).
The clothing also varies with national styles.
In East Asia it tends to follow local monastic dress, with the arms covered.

In India early depictions, especially from hotter regions, such as ___E:art of Mathura U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_of_Mathura)___ , Buddha is often shown with very thin robes or topless, with most of the body uncovered, or appearing so.
